def: The forebrain fails to split into left and right halves early in development. Causes midline face defects (single central incisor, close-set eyes, cleft lip, cyclopia in severe cases). Linked to Sonic hedgehog (SHH) mutations, trisomy 13 and fetal alcohol exposure.
Golden-brown rings around the edge of the cornea from copper deposits. Classic sign of Wilson disease (copper buildup in the body).
Inherited problem with getting rid of copper (ATP7B gene), so copper builds up in the liver, brain and eyes. Causes liver disease, movement and psychiatric problems, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear makes the face muscles twitch. A sign of low calcium (hypocalcemia).
Inflating a blood pressure cuff on the arm makes the hand and wrist spasm. A sign of low calcium. (Different from Trousseau syndrome, which is cancer-related clotting.)

term: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
def: The body releases too much ADH, so the kidneys hold on to water. Blood gets diluted, causing low sodium, while blood volume stays roughly normal. Causes include small cell lung cancer, CNS disease and some drugs.

Clotting gets switched on all over the body at once, which uses up platelets and clotting factors. Patients clot and bleed at the same time. Triggered by sepsis, trauma, obstetric problems and some cancers.

Widespread lung injury makes the tiny air sacs leaky and fill with fluid, so oxygen can't get into the blood. Low oxygen doesn't fix with extra O2. Triggered by sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma or pancreatitis.
Spoon-shaped nails: thin nails that curve up at the edges so they could hold a drop of water. Classically from iron deficiency anemia.
Trouble doing quick alternating movements, like flipping the hand back and forth. A sign of cerebellar damage on the same side.
Under the microscope, tumor cells line up in rows around areas of dead tissue. The classic look of glioblastoma.
Painless red-purple spots on the palms and soles from tiny infected clots. A sign of infective endocarditis.
Painful, raised red bumps on the finger and toe pads from immune complex deposits. A sign of infective endocarditis. (Mnemonic: Osler = Ouch.)
Retinal bleeds with pale centers, seen on eye exam. Classically linked to infective endocarditis.
Dark, thick, velvety skin in body folds such as the neck and armpits. Usually a sign of insulin resistance; rarely a sign of stomach cancer.
Heart attack: part of the heart muscle dies because its blood supply is blocked, usually by a clot on a ruptured plaque in a coronary artery.
Hormone from the posterior pituitary that makes the kidneys hold on to water (and constricts blood vessels at high levels). Released when blood is too concentrated or volume is low.
Long-term lung disease, usually from smoking, where airways are narrowed or air sacs destroyed, so air gets trapped and is hard to breathe out. Includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
Autoimmune disease where the body makes antibodies against its own DNA and cell parts, causing inflammation in skin, joints, kidneys, blood and more. Most common in young women.
Inherited (X-linked) lack of an enzyme that protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. Triggers like infections, fava beans or certain drugs cause red cells to burst (hemolysis).
Clear fluid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord. Made in the choroid plexus; sampled by lumbar puncture.
How much blood plasma the kidneys filter per minute. The main measure of kidney function; estimated from creatinine.
Pain and inflammation medicines (like ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin) that block COX enzymes and lower prostaglandins. Can cause stomach ulcers and kidney problems.
Deep, fast, labored breathing. The body's way of blowing off CO2 to correct metabolic acidosis, as in diabetic ketoacidosis.
Dangerous complication, mostly of type 1 diabetes: without insulin the body burns fat and makes acidic ketones. Causes high blood sugar, acidic blood, dehydration and Kussmaul breathing.
Pink needle-shaped crystals inside immature white blood cells (myeloblasts). Point to acute myeloid leukemia, especially APL.
A signaling protein that tells developing tissues where the midline is and patterns the brain, face and limbs. Mutations cause holoprosencephaly.
Fatty, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float. Means fat isn't being absorbed (pancreatic insufficiency, bile problems or gut disease).
Dark brown pigment the malaria parasite makes from leftover hemoglobin inside red blood cells.
An abnormally large tongue. Seen in hypothyroidism (cretinism), amyloidosis, acromegaly and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
